inlines.text: 就在科技巨头们加码投入之际，投资者却开始对 AI 基础设施支出感到不安。

blocks.text: 过去两周，Alphabet、亚马逊、Meta 和微软相继公布了今年的资本支出计划，合计超过 7400 亿美元。华尔街将其解读为 AI 基础设施支出，涵盖数据中心和芯片。

inlines.text: 过去两周，Alphabet、亚马逊、Meta 和微软相继公布了今年的资本支出计划，合计超过 7400 亿美元。华尔街将其解读为 AI 基础设施支出，涵盖数据中心和芯片。

blocks.text: 在 AI 热潮早期，投资者大多乐见这类巨额投入，将其视为对技术增长潜力有信心的信号。但进入第四季度后，这种热情似乎正在让位于对自由现金流为负（支出超过公司收入）、债务不断攀升，以及这些巨额投资究竟能否带来足够回报的担忧。

inlines.text: 在 AI 热潮早期，投资者大多乐见这类巨额投入，将其视为对技术增长潜力有信心的信号。但进入第四季度后，这种热情似乎正在让位于对自由现金流为负（支出超过公司收入）、债务不断攀升，以及这些巨额投资究竟能否带来足够回报的担忧。

blocks.text: 这种焦虑情绪周五蔓延至整个市场。纳斯达克指数下跌 2.9%，芯片股也遭到重创：英伟达跌 4%，博通跌逾 5%，高通跌 11%。Alphabet 周四暴跌 12%，创下有史以来最差单日表现，市值蒸发 5000 亿美元，周五再度下跌。

blocks.text: 担忧的一个重要原因在于，那些原本依靠核心业务拥有充裕自由现金流的公司，正因 AI 威胁到这些业务的经济性而受到冲击。Alphabet 本周提供了最清晰的例证。这家谷歌母公司公布第三季度自由现金流为负 91 亿美元，连续第二个季度告负，同期季度资本支出增至 514 亿美元。Alphabet 预计今年将支出高达 2050 亿美元，并预计 2027 年支出还将继续上升。

blocks.text: 与此同时，AI Mode——谷歌直接内置于搜索中的 AI 聊天机器人功能——的大获成功，正在侵蚀公司的摇钱树。谷歌的搜索广告业务约占其收入的一半，增速已放缓至 12%，为五个季度以来最慢。这让谷歌如履薄冰：它正斥资数十亿美元投入 AI 技术，而这项技术可能削弱为其贡献收入的搜索业务。

blocks.text: 亚马逊也处境相似，过去 12 个月自由现金流为负 424 亿美元，而上一财年为正 148 亿美元。公司表示今年资本支出预计为 2200 亿美元。尽管其云业务 AWS 收入增长 39%，亚马逊周四公布财报后股价仍大跌 7%。

blocks.text: Meta 同样在烧钱，第三季度自由现金流为负 21 亿美元，资本支出超过了经营现金流。公司预计今年资本支出最高达 1450 亿美元。该公司指出，其新推出的免费个人 AI 智能体 Muse 有点像无底洞（CEO 马克·扎克伯格曾说，它“运行起来非常消耗算力”）。但广告收入增长了 26%。尽管如此，再多的好消息也没能让 Meta 躲过上周股价 10% 的下跌。

blocks.text: 微软是自由现金流方面唯一的例外——最近一个季度录得正自由现金流 186 亿美元，资本支出为 452 亿美元，低于其此前预计的 500 亿美元。微软表示，这并非有意削减 AI 支出，而是归咎于第三方供应商的产能延迟。受此影响，出租 AI 算力的较小公司股价下跌。

blocks.text: 值得注意的是，支撑这一切 AI 基础设施的资金并不只来自大型科技公司的利润，还体现在股票和债券的发行上。据标普全球市场情报的数据，微软、Alphabet、亚马逊、Meta 和甲骨文在 2026 年合计发债 3260 亿美元，是去年发债规模的三倍。

blocks.text: 市场对 AI 算力的需求依然强劲。谷歌、亚马逊和微软的云业务均实现增长，但满足这些需求的成本正让投资者感到不安。

blocks.text: 这种不明朗的局面可能让 Anthropic 备受期待的 IPO 变得更加复杂。这家 AI 公司本周早些时候提交了上市申请，而其未来的增长取决于能否获得海量算力。英国《金融时报》周五报道称，黑石已提醒投资者，该公司在 IPO 后可能无法获得投资级评级，这意味着它可能不得不更加依赖超大规模云服务商和第三方来为其基础设施雄心提供资金。

blocks.text: Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down.

inlines.text: Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down.

blocks.text: Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips.

inlines.text: Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips.

blocks.text: Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns.

inlines.text: Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns.

blocks.text: The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again.

inlines.text: The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again.

blocks.text: A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027.

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it.

blocks.text: Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday.

The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday.

blocks.text: Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week.

blocks.text: Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank.

blocks.text: It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year.

blocks.text: Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand.

blocks.text: These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions.
